claims.sentence: Spirometry is the most common lung function test.
claims.evidence: Retrieved review text calls spirometry the most commonly used lung function test (non-UK academic source).

claims.sentence: It measures how much air the lungs can hold and how quickly air can be blown out.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text: spirometry measures how much and how fast air can be exhaled; lung volumes need a separate lung volume test.
claims.newSentence: It measures how much air a person can blow out and how quickly.

claims.sentence: Lung function tests give an indication of the capacity of the lungs and how clear the airways are.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: spirometry is the main test for airflow obstruction; wider lung function tests assess lung volumes and gas exchange. Wording 'capacity ... how clear airways' not found.
claims.newSentence: Spirometry is the main test for detecting airflow obstruction, while other lung function tests measure lung volumes and gas exchange.

claims.sentence: The person wears a nose clip so air goes through the mouth, and breathes through a mouthpiece into the lung function machine.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: nose clip or holding the nose, lips sealed around mouthpiece.

claims.sentence: They breathe normally, take a deep breath in, and then blow out as hard and fast as possible.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: deep breath in, then a forceful, fast breath out until the lungs feel empty.

claims.sentence: Each blow is repeated at least three times, with enough rest in between.
claims.evidence: 'At least three times' not found in retrieved text; one source says you may have to repeat the manoeuvre a number of times.
claims.newSentence: Each blow may be repeated several times, with rests in between.

claims.sentence: The test usually takes about 15 minutes.
claims.evidence: One NHS trust leaflet: the whole test normally takes around 15 minutes; others say 10 to 30 minutes.
claims.newSentence: One NHS trust says the test normally takes around 15 minutes.

claims.sentence: One NHS practice suggests avoiding vigorous exercise for 30 minutes before the test.
claims.evidence: Retrieved NHS sources: avoid vigorous exercise for about 30 minutes before.

claims.sentence: The same guidance suggests wearing loose clothing, removing loose-fitting dentures and chewing gum, and emptying the bladder.
claims.evidence: Loose clothing retrieved; dentures, chewing gum and bladder not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The same guidance suggests wearing loose clothing.

claims.sentence: It also asks people to tell staff about a recent chest infection that needed antibiotics or steroids, or a heart attack in the last three months.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: recent antibiotics or steroids can affect results; recent coughing up blood or surgery can make testing unsuitable. 'Heart attack in last three months' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: It also notes that a recent chest infection, or recent antibiotics or steroids, can affect the results.

claims.sentence: Practices differ, so the appointment letter has the exact instructions.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: stopping times for inhalers vary by drug and patients are told if they need to stop medicines; 'appointment letter' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Preparation varies, and patients are told whether they need to stop any inhalers or medicines beforehand.

claims.sentence: The test is often repeated after a reliever inhaler to check whether it helps the airways.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: the repeat-after-inhaler test is sometimes done to investigate asthma or when the diagnosis is unclear, not always 'often'.
claims.newSentence: The test is sometimes repeated after a reliever inhaler to check whether it helps the airways.

claims.sentence: The person takes the test, uses the inhaler, waits a short time and repeats the test.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: spirometry, then inhaler, a pause (10 to 40 minutes depending on the trust and medicine), then repeat.

claims.sentence: A clear improvement suggests that the airways respond to the medicine, which supports a diagnosis of asthma.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: the comparison shows how much airways respond to medicine and helps check whether the inhaler helps breathing. 'Supports a diagnosis of asthma' not retrieved; NICE says a single normal result does not rule out asthma.
claims.newSentence: The comparison shows how much the airways respond to the medicine, and the test is sometimes used when asthma is being investigated.

claims.sentence: Results are compared with predicted values for someone of the same height, age and sex.
claims.evidence: Cornwall NHS guideline: predicted values are calculated from height, age and sex.

claims.sentence: The laboratory report shows the reference values used for the comparison.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: a typical report shows measured values, predicted values and percent predicted; 'reference values used' not specifically retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A typical report shows the measured values alongside the predicted values.

claims.sentence: In obstructive conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), the airways narrow, making it harder for air to flow out of the lungs.
claims.evidence: StatPearls/PMC: obstructive diseases raise resistance to airflow through partial or complete airway blockage; spirometry diagnoses asthma and COPD.

claims.sentence: Restrictive conditions are different, because they decrease the amount of air the lungs can hold.
claims.evidence: StatPearls: restrictive disorders have smaller lung volumes, mainly lower total lung capacity.

claims.sentence: A respiratory doctor reviews the results and, if needed, arranges a follow-up appointment to explain them.
claims.evidence: Royal Wolverhampton leaflet: results are discussed at the next clinic appointment with the consultant or GP. 'Respiratory doctor arranges follow-up' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: One NHS leaflet says results are discussed at the next clinic appointment with the consultant or GP.

claims.sentence: If no follow-up is needed, the results go directly to the GP.
claims.evidence: Direct routing of results to the GP not found.

claims.sentence: NHS leaflets say there are no direct risks from lung function tests.
claims.evidence: Retrieved NHS leaflets mention dizziness or fainting, and rare serious complications (airway narrowing, collapsed lung); not 'no risks'.
claims.newSentence: NHS leaflets describe the test as painless and non-invasive, with dizziness or fainting the most common side effects and more serious complications very rare.

claims.sentence: The effort can be tiring, and people are given time to recover between tests.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: exertion required can cause dizziness or fainting; 'tiring' and recovery time not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The test needs a good effort, which can make some people feel dizzy or faint.

claims.sentence: Some people feel dizzy or faint, and coughing is common.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: some patients feel dizzy or faint; coughing is common.

claims.sentence: In spirometry the person breathes through a mouthpiece, with a nose clip, into a machine that measures airflow.
claims.evidence: Nose clip and mouthpiece into a spirometer (retrieved).

claims.sentence: Each blow is repeated at least three times, with rests in between.
claims.evidence: 'At least three times' not found.
claims.newSentence: Each blow may be repeated several times, with rests in between.

claims.sentence: Results are compared with values predicted for someone of the same height, age and sex.
claims.evidence: Cornwall NHS guideline: predicted values from height, age and sex.

claims.sentence: The test may be repeated after a reliever inhaler to see whether the airways open up.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: sometimes repeated after an inhaler to see whether it helps breathing.
claims.newSentence: The test may be repeated after a reliever inhaler to see whether it helps breathing.

claims.sentence: Spirometry measures how much air the lungs hold and how fast it can be blown out. This guide covers the test, preparation and what results are compared with.
claims.evidence: Spirometry measures air blown out and its speed, not how much the lungs hold.
claims.newSentence: Spirometry measures how much air can be blown out and how fast. This guide covers the test, preparation and what results are compared with.

notes: Extra facts: spirometry measures how much and how fast air is exhaled (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10679964/); NICE says a single normal spirometry result does not rule out asthma (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/htg776/documents/final-scope); NHS leaflets list stopping times for inhalers varying by drug (https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/spirometry/); rare serious complications exist but dizziness/fainting are most common (https://www.wsh.nhs.uk/CMS-Documents/Patient-leaflets/RespiratoryMedicine/5048-3LungFunction(Breathing)Tests.pdf). The nhs.uk spirometry page itself was not retrieved verbatim; search summaries are lossy.
